name: Freya Ito

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal workday look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead the small town choir, play piano for its rehearsals and teach private voice pupils. I have a master’s degree in music and can bring a rough group into tune, but the choir budget pays less than a lead job usually would.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What follows you home after rehearsal?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The hall keys and the question of whether every singer got home safely. My partner and I have two school-age children and a mortgage; there is less than a month of expenses in our savings account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the choir committee that a quicker mailing list is no reason to cut a rehearsal. The singers still need someone to hear the wrong note and show them where to breathe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I already worry about a cancelled concert because my pay is low and our reserve is under a month. There are few nearby choirs with a paid lead seat, so a plateau does not make the mortgage easier.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I would keep leading choir rehearsal and the six voice pupils who pay for lessons. I would ask the committee for the next quarter’s paid rehearsal dates in writing before setting childcare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious even in a quiet AI future. One unpaid fortnight would reach the mortgage before a new job appeared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Has a rehearsal gone unpaid before?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The committee cancelled one winter night when the hall heat failed and paid nothing. I would ask for a written cancellation fee before the next term.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where could you trim now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would postpone the family weekend away if another choir fee went missing. I would not cut the children’s instrument hire first.

I would request a **cancellation fee** before the next choir term.
think: Our **under-one-month reserve** makes an unpaid fortnight serious.
Few **nearby choir jobs** offer a quick replacement for this low-paid lead role.
do: Keep **choir rehearsals** and six paid voice pupils this week.
Request **written paid dates** and a cancellation fee before the next term.
Postpone the **family weekend** if another choir fee disappears.
feel: I feel **anxious** about existing income gaps and the mortgage.
S0.quote: One unpaid fortnight would reach the mortgage before a new job appeared.
fieldNote: Her **thin reserve** and scarce similar jobs sustain anxiety even without strong AI change.
She would protect **instrument hire** while postponing a family weekend after a lost fee.

steps.text: Keep choir rehearsals and six paid voice pupils this week
Request written paid rehearsal dates and cancellation fee before next term
Postpone family weekend if another choir fee disappears

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the committee that software can print a practice line, but it cannot judge a timid singer’s breath. I would ask them to keep a paid rehearsal leader in the budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Preparing rehearsal recordings and written parts gives me nearly a quarter of my pay. If cheap software takes those fees, I cannot fill the gap with one more pupil, and I know how little we have saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next month I would show the committee what the paid part-preparation hours actually cover and request a written contract for them. If those hours are cut in the first year, I would keep my voice pupils and apply for a posted paid music-centre leader job only if my master’s degree qualifies, the written net pay after travel replaces the lost fees and school pickup fits; I would stay until an offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about the preparation fees, and alarmed if the choir also cut my paid rehearsals. I cannot use the mortgage money to buy myself an experiment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try the committee’s AI score maker?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not with a child’s voice or name in it. I have never used AI, and I would need a paid lesson, local storage approval and a way to check every note by ear before I tested my own nameless part.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Are there many suitable openings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There are few. I would answer a real posting, not leave my choir job because someone heard of a possible vacancy.

I would apply for a **real paid opening** if those hours fall.

feel: I feel **anxious** about lost preparation fees.
S1.quote: I cannot use the mortgage money to buy myself an experiment.
fieldNote: She expects **preparation fees** to shrink first; she does not yet commit to learning AI.
A **different lead role** needs lost fees, a real opening, degree eligibility, better written net pay and pickup.

steps.text: Keep choir rehearsals and pupils while preparation hours remain paid

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the choir committee that AGI by 2028 can make parts and rehearsal tracks quickly. They still have to tell me, in writing, whether a person will be paid to lead the room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the preparation fees to vanish in 2028 and fear the committee may buy fewer led rehearsals. Robots able to play and sing physically arrive around 2031, three years later, but I could lose work much sooner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I would total my preparation invoices and ask for a signed rehearsal schedule. In the first year after 2028, if paid rehearsals also fall, I would apply for a posted arts-centre voice tutor role only if my degree qualifies, written net pay after travel covers the lost choir fees and the hours fit child pickup; I would keep pupils and choir calls until a written offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be alarmed. If preparation and rehearsals both shrink, most of my own pay goes, and I have already lain awake counting the next mortgage instalment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay for a new teaching certificate now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if a posted role actually requires it and a funded place or paid study time exists. I cannot spend the last month of our household reserve on tuition.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the arts centre says a post may open soon?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep working and ask them to send the actual posting. A rumour cannot tell me hours or wages.

say: I would demand a **signed rehearsal schedule** before promising evenings.
I would pursue a **posted voice tutor post** if paid rehearsals fall.
think: My **preparation fees** likely end in 2028 before 2031 robots.

do: Total **preparation invoices** and request signed rehearsal dates now.
Apply for a **posted tutor role** after 2028 rehearsal cuts only if qualified, written net after travel covers losses and pickup fits.
Keep **pupils and choir calls** until a suitable written offer is signed.
feel: I feel **alarmed** by likely large losses and mortgage worry.
S2.quote: A rumour cannot tell me hours or wages.
fieldNote: Her **2028 preparation loss** arrives before capable physical robots around 2031.
The **voice tutor move** requires actual rehearsal cuts, a posted opening, eligibility, written net pay, pickup and signed offer.

steps.text: Apply for qualified posted tutor after 2028 cuts; written net after travel covers fees, pickup fits
Keep pupils and paid choir calls until suitable written offer is signed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the choir families that five years until AGI by 2031 is time to see whether they will pay for a smaller singing group. I would not promise a free class every Saturday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Parts and tracks may stop paying by 2031, but a paid group could replace some fees if there is enough demand. Singing robots may arrive around 2034; I cannot bank on the old choir budget forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This autumn I would offer a six-week family singing group only if the hall gives us a room after child pickup and ten families prepay enough for rent, a paid accompanist, my teaching and preparation time. In the first year after 2031 I would repeat only if ten places still pay those costs and the hall and pickup remain; otherwise I would continue my six private lessons.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious until the group pays the accompanist and me. With less than a month saved, I cannot float even one unpaid singing class.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you run it if six families sign up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Six fees do not pay both musicians or the hall. I would refund them and keep the regular pupils rather than borrow for rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the hall has no room after pickup?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not move the class to a late hour that leaves our children stranded. I would wait for a suitable room and keep teaching privately.

Keep **six private pupils** and refund six deposits if group fees fail.

S3.quote: With less than a month saved, I cannot float even one unpaid singing class.
fieldNote: The **group gate** is ten prepaid families covering hall rent and both musicians’ teaching and preparation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the choir that a decade until AGI by 2036 gives us time to write down what live rehearsals are worth. We should not treat volunteers as a substitute for wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I may lose the preparation fees by 2036 and face singing robots around 2039. The longer runway helps, but our thin reserve is a problem this year, not just in ten years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting this term I would ask the committee for a written two-year paid rehearsal contract and set aside five percent of each extra paid lesson fee after food and the mortgage, aiming for three months saved. In the first year after 2036 I would continue the choir only while rehearsals pay and apply for a posted regional conductor role only if my master’s degree qualifies, written net pay after travel covers lost choir fees and pickup works; I would leave only after a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would remain anxious because a contract renewal can fail long before 2036. A small savings rule gives us a little control when a lesson actually pays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if there are no extra lesson fees?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I save nothing new that week. I will not call money already needed for groceries a savings plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move towns for a title?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only for a real written offer whose net pay and hours work for our family. A title without pay does not clear the mortgage.

I would consider a **regional conductor opening** only with workable pay and hours.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because preparation fees and paid rehearsals might disappear before another real post opens. Written choir dates, a posted qualified job with take-home pay and reliable pickup would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether singers are paying the accompanist too. If two musicians make a class happen, both need a fee.

headlineQuote: If two musicians make a class happen, both need a fee.
portrait: At **43**, Freya leads a choir and teaches voice with a music master’s degree, two children and a mortgage.
Her **lower pay**, under-one-month reserve and few local posts make even a plateau anxious.
She has **never used AI** and would need paid instruction and strict privacy before testing a score tool.
A **paid singing group** needs ten prepaid families, a room after pickup and fees for both musicians.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could erase preparation fees and cut paid rehearsals before another job opens.
whatWouldHelp: **Written choir dates**, a posted qualified role with sufficient net pay and reliable child pickup would help Freya.
